<poem>{{smaller block|One hath wounded me,
That’s by me wounded; ''both'' our remedies
Within thy help and holy physic lies.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 3.]}}}}</poem>

'''Both two, both the two,''' {{smaller|pleonastically for ''both''.}}
{{smaller block|''Both the two'' cities reached a high pitch of prosperity.
{{right|''Grote'', Hist. Greece, ii. 18.}}}}

'''both''' (bōth), ''adv.'' or ''conj.'' [< ME. ''bothe'', ''bothen'', ''bathe'', etc.; from the adj.] Including the two (terms or notions mentioned): an adverb preceding two coördinate terms (words or phrases) joined by ''and'', and standing thus in an apparent conjunctional correlation, ''both'' . . . ''and'', equivalent to ''not only'' . . . ''but also''. ''Both'' is thus used sometimes before three or more coördinate terms.
{{smaller block|I thought good now to present vnto your Grace not any better gift of mine owne, . . . but surely an excellent gift of an other mans deuise and making, which ''both'' hath done, doth, ''and'' shal do much good to many other good folke, ''and'' to your Noble Grace also.
{{right|''John Fouler'', Pref. to Sir T. More’s Cumfort against}}
{{right|[Tribulation (1573).}}}}
{{smaller block|[He] was indeed his country’s ''both'' minion, mirror, ''and'' wonder.
{{right|''Ford'', Line of Life.}}}}
{{smaller block|A great multitude ''both'' of the Jews ''and'' also of the Greeks believed.
{{right|Acts xiv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Which I suppose they doe resigne with much willingness, ''both'' Livery, Badge, ''and'' Cognizance.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxi.}}}}
{{smaller block|But these discourses were ''both'' written ''and'' delivered in the freshness of his complete manhood.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Emerson, v.}}}}

It belongs to the group of the ''Pseudophyllidea'' (which see). Also ''Botryocephalus.''

'''bothrium''' (both′ri-um), ''n.''; pl. ''bothria'' (-ä̤). [NL., < Gr. βοθρίον, a small trench, dim. of βόθρος, a pit, trench.] One of the facets or fossettes upon the head of a tapeworm.

'''bother''' (boᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''v.''   [First in the early part of the 18th century, also written ''bodder'', Sc. ''bauther'', ''bather''; origin unknown; possibly a corruption of ''pother''. The earliest instances seem to be from Swift and other Irishmen, which would seem to favor the supposed Ir. derivation, < Ir. ''buaidhrim'', I vex, disturb (cf. ''buaidhirt'', trouble, affliction); but the Ir. words as pronounced have no resemblance to ''bother'', except as to the initial ''b''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To bewilder; confuse.
{{smaller block|With the din of which tube my head you so ''bother''.
{{right|''T. Sheridan'', To Swift.}}}}
'''2.''' To give trouble to; annoy; pester; worry.
{{smaller block|Dunsey ''bothered'' me for the money, and I let him have it.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Silas Marner, ix.}}}}
{{smaller block|He ''bothered'' his audience with no accidental effects.
{{right|''Stedman'', Poets of America, p. 280.}}}}
{{smaller block|[Used in the imperative as an expression of impatience, or as a mild sort of execration.
''Bother'' the woman for plaguing me!{{right|''Farrar''.]}}}}
='''Syn.''' {{smaller|''Pester'', ''Worry'', etc. See ''tease'', ''v. t.''}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To trouble one’s self; make many words or much ado: as, don’t ''bother'' about that.

'''bother''' (boᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bother'', ''v.'']   '''1†.''' Blarney; humbug; palaver. ''N. E. D.''—'''2.''' Trouble; vexation; plague: as, what a ''bother'' it is!
{{smaller block|The ''bother'' with Mr. Emerson is, that, though he writes in prose, he is essentially a poet.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 376.}}}}
{{smaller block|At night, they [the ponies] were a ''bother''; if picketed out, they fed badly and got thin, and if they were not picketed, they sometimes strayed away.
{{right|''The Century'', XXX. 223.}}}}

'''botheration''' (boᴛ̵ʜ-e̤-rā′shon), ''n.''   [< ''bother'' + ''-ation.'']   The act of bothering, or the state of being bothered; annoyance; trouble; vexation; perplexity.
{{smaller block|A man must have a good stomach that can swallow this ''botheration'' [autograph albums] as a compliment.
{{right|''Scott'', Diary, Nov. 20, 1825.}}}}
{{smaller block|Their smallness, their folly, their rascality, and their simple power of ''botheration.''
{{right|''Caroline Fox'', Journal, p. 250.}}}}

'''botherer''' (boᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ėr), ''n.'' One who bothers, vexes, or annoys: as, “such ''botherers'' of judges,” ''Warren.''

'''botherment''' (boᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ment), ''n.''   [< ''bother'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of bothering or the state of being bothered; trouble; annoyance; botheration. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|I’m sure ’t would be a ''botherment'' to a living soul to lose so much money. {{right|''J. F. Cooper.''}}}}

'''bothersome''' (boᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sum), ''a.''   [< ''bother'' + ''-some.'']   Troublesome; annoying; inconvenient.
{{smaller block|By his ''bothersome'' questioning of all traditional assumptions. {{right|''The American'', VII. 235.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [casements] open sidewise, in two wings, and are screwed together by that ''bothersome'' little iron handle over which we have fumbled so often in European inns.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Portraits of Places, p. 353.}}}}

'''both-handedness''' (bōth′han″ded-nes), ''n.'' The power of using either hand with equal ease; ambidexterity.
{{smaller block|The tendency toward what might be called ''both-handedness'' in the use of the brush. {{right|''The Student'', III. 284.}}}}

'''both-hands†''' (bōth′handz), ''n.'' A person indispensable to another; a factotum.
{{smaller block|He is his master’s ''both-hands'', I assure you. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|To accept the hospitality of a very poor Highland ''bothie.''
{{right|''The Century'', XXVII. 919.}}}}
'''2.''' A house for the accommodation of a number of workpeople in the employment of the same person or company. {{smaller|More especially, a kind of barrack in connection with a large farm, where the unmarried outdoor servants and laborers are lodged.—'''Bothy system''', the practice, common in Aberdeenshire and other northern counties of Scotland, of lodging the unmarried outdoor servants and laborers employed on the larger farms in barrack-like buildings apart from their employer’s residence.}}

'''botoné''' (bot′on-ā), ''a.'' Same as ''bottony''.

'''bo-tree''' (bō′trē), ''n.''   [< Singhalese ''bo'' (also ''bogaha'' : ''gaha'', tree), a shortened form of Pali ''bodhi'', the bo-tree, short for ''bodhi-taru'', bo-tree (< ''bodhi'' (< Skt. ''bodhi''), wisdom, enlightenment, + ''taru'', tree), answering to Skt. ''bodhi-vriksha'' (''vriksha'', tree). See ''Buddha''.]   The ''Ficus religiosa'', or pipul-tree, under which Sakyamuni, the founder of Buddhism, is said to have become “enlightened” (Buddha), after forty days’ fixed contemplation, during which time he was subjected to all manner of temptation, and to have evolved the four noble truths by which mankind may be delivered from the miseries attending upon birth, life, and death. {{smaller|The particular bo-tree under which this happened is said to have been produced at the moment of his birth.}}

'''Botrychium''' (bo-trik′i-um), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. βότρυχος, equiv. to βόστρυχος, a curl or lock, a cluster: see ''Bostrychus''.]   A genus of cryptogamous plants, natural order ''Ophioglossaceæ'', allied to the ferns. {{smaller|They bear clustered, veinless sporangia in contracted panicled spikes above the variously divided frond. There are several widely distributed species, known by the popular name of ''moonwort'', from the crescent shape of the divisions of the frond in some common kinds. The name ''grape-fern'' is also given to them, and one species, ''B. Virginianum'', is called ''rattlesnake-fern''.}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0663 c3f1.png|width=176px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Moonwort (''Botrychium Lunaria''). ''a'', entire plant; ''b'', branch of the fertile frond, showing sporangia.}}}}

'''botryllid''' (bo-tril′id), ''n.'' A tunicate of the family ''Botryllidæ''.

'''Botryllidæ''' (bo-tril′i-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Botryllus'' + ''-idæ''.]   A family of compound ascidians or tunicaries, of the order ''Ascidioidea''. {{smaller|They have a definite number of ascidiozoöids grouped about a common cloaca of the ascidiarium, the viscera of each single body, which is not divided into thorax and abdomen, lying by the side of the respiratory cavity, and no lobes around the inhalent orifice. There are several genera besides ''Botryllus''. Also ''Botryllacea'' and ''Botrylloides''.}}

'''Botryllus''' (bo-tril′us), ''n.''   [NL., dim. of Gr. βότρυς, a cluster or bunch of grapes, a curl or lock.]   A genus of compound ascidians, typical of the family ''Botryllidæ''. ''B. stellatus'' and ''B. violaceus'' are examples.

'''Botryocephalus''' (bot″ri-ọ̄-sef′a-lus), ''n.'' Same as ''Bothriocephalus''. ''Oken'', 1815.

'''botryogen''' (bot′ri-ọ̄-jen), ''n.''   [< Gr. βότρυς, a cluster of grapes, + -γενής, producing, etc.: see ''-gen''.]   A red or ocher-yellow mineral from Falun in Sweden, consisting of the hydrous sulphates of iron, magnesium, and calcium.

'''botryoid, botryoidal''' (bot′ri-oid, bot-ri-oi′dạl), ''a.''   [< Gr. βοτρυοειδής, like a cluster of grapes, < βότρυς, a cluster of grapes, + εἶδος, form.]   Having the {{img float|file=century v01 p0663 c3f2.png|width=212px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Botryoidal structure: Chalcedony.}}}} form of a bunch of grapes; like grapes, as a mineral presenting an aggregation of small globes. {{smaller|In ''bot.'', applied to forms of inflorescence which are apparently botryose, but in reality cymose.}}

'''botryoidally''' (bot-ri-oi′dạl-i), ''adv.'' In a botryoidal manner; so as to resemble a bunch of grapes: as, vessels ''botryoidally'' disposed.

'''botryolite''' (bot′ri-ọ̄-līt), ''n.''   [< Gr. βότρυς, a cluster of grapes, + λίθος, a stone.]   A variety of datolite or borosilicate of calcium, occurring in mammillary or botryoidal concretions, in a bed of magnetic iron in gneiss, near Arendal in Norway, and elsewhere. {{smaller|Its colors are pearl-gray, grayish- or reddish-white, and pale rose-red. It is said to}} differ from datolite in containing more water.
